title: Satisfying Quantum Codes: Physics-Informed and Hardware-Aware Code Design with SAT Solvers
authors: Ben DalFavero, William M. Watkins, Margarite L. LaBorde, Vincent Russo, Ethan Egger, Gregory Quiroz, Ryan LaRose
abstract: Although quantum error correction is widely believed to be necessary for impactful applications of quantum computers, the design of quantum error correction codes is largely done by hand, without respect to problem or hardware constraints. In this work, we present a highly general and flexible framework for the computational design of both physics-inspired and hardware-aware quantum codes. To do so, we formulate code design as a Boolean satisfiability (SAT) problem and show how to incorporate all required error correction criteria. We prove that code design is NP-complete, ruling out any efficient algorithm for designing codes in general. Nonetheless, we show that state-of-the-art SAT solvers are able to effectively find solutions for many practical problems. Notably, we are able to design physics-inspired codes with up to 100 physical qubits in minutes, and we design new hardware-aware codes for biased noise which have a lower logical error rate than state-of-the-art surface codes.
summary: This paper introduces a powerful, general framework for designing quantum error correction codes by reformulating the design problem as a Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problem. By using state-of-the-art SAT solvers, the authors can computationally discover codes that respect specific physical symmetries or are tailored to realistic hardware noise profiles. This advances the practical feasibility of building fault-tolerant quantum computers.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of designing quantum error correction (QEC) codes, which is currently done manually without considering specific physical or hardware constraints.
main_result: They developed a general framework that formulates code design as a Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problem, successfully designing novel, hardware-aware codes with lower error rates than state-of-the-art surface codes.
method: The core method involves translating the code design problem (including constraints from physics or noise models) into a SAT problem and leveraging state-of-the-art SAT solvers to find solutions.
model_or_system: The work focuses on quantum stabilizer codes, which are used to protect quantum information. The framework is general enough to incorporate physics-inspired symmetries, such as those derived from the Fermi-Hubbard model, and detailed noise models.
key_observables: Logical error rate, satisfiability probability (PSAT), and the ability to encode up to 100 physical qubits.
important_parameters: Code parameters $[[n, k, d]]$, code-design density $m/(n-k)$, and the number of physical qubits ($n$).
main_assumptions: The general problem is proven to be NP-complete, meaning an efficient algorithm for all cases is unlikely, and the approach relies on the practical effectiveness of modern SAT solvers.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the code design framework overview, the phase transition in satisfiability probability vs. error parameter, and comparisons showing reduced logical error rates for novel codes under biased noise.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the framework, proves the NP-completeness of the problem, details the SAT formulation for code discovery and extension, and validates the method by applying it to physics-inspired and hardware-aware noise models.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it provides a computational, systematic methodology for designing robust quantum hardware components (QEC codes) by mapping a complex physical problem onto a well-studied computational problem (SAT).

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of our quantum code design framework. Our framework enables two categories of code design: code discovery and code extension. In the former, the code is initialized with an empty stabilizer set, while in the latter the initial set S0 is determined by a predetermined code or a set of physics-informed symmetries captured within the Hamiltonian H. Our SAT-based framework enables translation between both code design scenarios through the symplectic form, which encodes information about both the error set E and stabilizers/symmetries. Figure 2. Illustration of distance-increasing extensions of quantum codes with mutation, shown here for two QLDPC codes. (a) A distance d = 3 rotated surface code overlaid on a d = 5 distance surface code. (b) A distance d = 3 tri- angular color code (the Steane code) overlaid on a distance d = 5 triangular color code. Note that, in both cases, there are checks along the boundary of the smaller code that must be altered. Thus, these are examples of distance-increasing extensions with mutation.

Figure 3. Demonstration of the SAT–UNSAT phase tran- sition which we empirically observe for random instances of k-code design (Def. 3). The order parameter is the number of errors per stabilizer m/(n −k) in the code design problem. In addition to the transition in satisfiability probability pSAT at the critical value, the solve time peaks at this critical value. Additional numerical results and cases are discussed in detail in Appendix D.

Figure 4. Predicted existence of [[n, k, 3]] stabilizer codes as a function of the number of physical qubits n and logical qubits k. Dark blue denotes parameters for which code existence is guaranteed by the quantum Gilbert–Varshamov bound, while dark red denotes parameters excluded by the quantum Singleton bound. In the intermediate region, the empirical scaling model for the critical error-set size bmc(n, k, w), with w = d −1 = 2, predicts satisfiable (light blue) and unsatisfi- able (light red) k-Code Design instances.
